source.title: Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own scaling experiments and examines how fitting and evaluation choices affect the resulting compute frontiers, but on AlphaZero Hex performance rather than language-model loss.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy, parameter/token scaling, or downstream language-model performance. Its own Hex performance-scaling results and comparisons of frontier fits are recorded; the cited language-model scaling results are not.
record.test_reason: The study trains AlphaZero Hex agents and fits Elo-versus-compute frontiers with a change-point model (sigmoid-like, Elo linear in log compute). That is game-playing performance in multi-agent RL, not held-out loss. So it does not measure what V1–V4 or V6 name, nor the power-law loss form V5 names. Its fitting-form and evaluation-method comparisons (r8, r9) concern Hex Elo frontiers, not the language-model exponents or compute-optimal splits in V7. All findings are a related construct and go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Add three points. The authors say compute frontiers are exponential in desired performance and again in board size. Performance changes smoothly with compute and board size, with no spikes. Small-problem relationships carry over to problems orders of magnitude costlier, though they note this may be specific to Hex.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains AlphaZero agents by self-play on Hex and fits Elo-versus-compute frontiers; it does not use language-model pretraining or held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The top-agent evaluation produces noisier frontiers than league evaluation, although the authors report similar form and fits. The study also compares linear, sigmoid, and change-point curve forms.

fits_no_version.finding: Hex AlphaZero Elo frontiers follow a sigmoid/change-point shape in training compute, with an incline of about 500 Elo per 10x compute (Table III).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In two-player RL games, playing strength rises linearly in log training compute between a random-play plateau and perfect play.

fits_no_version.finding: Compute for perfect play rises 7x per board-size increment and takeoff compute rises 4x. The random-to-perfect gap grows by 500 Elo per increment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute frontiers shift exponentially and predictably with problem size in Hex.

fits_no_version.finding: Frontiers fitted on small boards predict larger-board frontiers. Residual variance decays exponentially as boards are added (Fig. 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling behaviour extrapolates across problem size in Hex.

fits_no_version.finding: Each extra 10x of train compute removes about 15x of test-time search compute at fixed Elo, down to a one-node floor (Fig. 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Train-time and test-time compute trade off log-linearly in AlphaZero Hex.

fits_no_version.finding: Change-point and sigmoid fits have similar MSE and linear fits are distorted at the curve ends. Top-agent evaluation gives noisier frontiers with similar form; parameters shift somewhat (slope 510 vs 600).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hex frontier conclusions are robust to fitting form and evaluation method.

record.problems: The study is limited to Hex and a custom AlphaZero implementation; the authors state that they lack a good baseline for its training speed. Some frontier comparisons are figure-based, and the top-agent evaluation is explicitly noisier. The study does not measure language-model loss.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for each board size's plotted frontier were extracted because the figures provide curves without textual values for each size; see Figures 5–7. Figure 8's individual checkpoint curves are also not separately extracted; r7 records the stated aggregate finding.

untested.parts: Whether the power-law loss form holds outside text pretraining. The study measures Elo frontiers in RL board games, not loss, and its fitted form is a clamped linear-in-log-compute change-point model.
Dependence of LM loss exponents or compute-optimal parameter/token splits on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 limits_scope label is removed: the rows measure Hex Elo-frontier fitting, not the LM scaling-law quantities V7 names. The study's frontier form (clamped linear in log compute) is not a power law in loss. If the claim set ever adds an RL or game-performance version, this study would be a T3 test with supporting results.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger language-model runs from smaller runs. The study predicts frontiers at larger board sizes from smaller board sizes instead.
Architecture effects on loss at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds for loss in other modalities or training regimes; the study measures Hex playing performance, not loss.
Downstream task performance predicted from pretraining loss or language-model scale.
Whether language-model loss exponents or compute-optimal parameter/token splits depend on setup. The study compares Hex frontier fitting choices, not those quantities.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Alternative curve-fitting forms and evaluation methods for Hex frontiers
reader_labels.reason: Frontier fit results vary in noisiness and the authors compare multiple functional forms, but the change-point and sigmoid fits have similar MSE and top-agent evaluation gives a similar form and fit; see r8 and r9. This does not establish language-model exponent or allocation sensitivity.
